## Villavante as a Mirror: What Almuñécar Could Learn

In the Leonese town of Villavante, on the banks of the Órbigo river, a ritual that is now in its thirty-ninth edition is repeated every first weekend of August. Bell ringers from Asturias, Cantabria, Galicia, Castilla y León, and occasionally other regions, climb the parish church tower to take turns ringing the bells manually, exchange techniques, and, above all, make themselves visible to a crowd that packs the square. The gathering began in 1986 as a modest initiative by a group of locals concerned about the disappearance of traditional ringing, and over the decades it has become a benchmark event for bell ringing in the northwest of the Iberian Peninsula.

What happens in Villavante is not a simple folkloric act nor an exhibition for clueless tourists. The organizers insist that the main goal is to build a new generation: each edition brings in young people who have never held a rope and who, after two or three summers, end up taking on responsibilities in their own bell towers. The formula combines practical workshops in the mornings, collective ringing at midday, and a brotherhood meal that serves as an informal space for oral transmission. Veteran bell ringers share anecdotes, correct postures, teach the specific rhythms of each valley, and answer questions that no written manual could ever cover.

Almuñécar lacks an equivalent event, and that absence weighs more heavily than it might seem at first glance. The bell ringers of Almuñécar who still hold the knowledge of local ringing have never been invited to share it in an organized setting, either within the municipality or at gatherings in other regions. There is no date on the calendar that brings them together, puts them in front of a microphone, or presents them to new generations as custodians of valuable knowledge. The contrast with Villavante is eloquent: there, the tradition is celebrated, practiced, and renewed every year; here, it is quietly fading away, confined to the memory of a few and to bells that barely ring anymore.

Visibility, or its absence, largely determines the health of intangible heritage. An annual gathering like the one in León serves a dual purpose: it socially legitimizes the activity in the eyes of the locals and attracts curious onlookers who would otherwise never consider learning to ring. In Almuñécar, the lack of a similar space has turned manual bell ringing into an invisible, almost clandestine practice, one that only emerges at funerals or on certain holidays when the automation fails. The local bell ringers do not feel recognized, and potential apprentices do not even know there is something to learn.

The Villavante model demonstrates that large budgets or complex infrastructures are not needed to reverse a trend of decline. All it takes is an accessible tower, a group of people willing to organize, and the willingness to open the doors to anyone who shows interest. The gatherings are funded by modest contributions from participants and the occasional support of the neighborhood council, and yet they have managed to keep alive a network of bell ringers that spans dozens of towns. The key lies in continuity: thirty-nine years of uninterrupted calls have created a habit, an expectation, and a sense of belonging that transcends specific individuals.

Almuñécar could look into this mirror without needing to copy the exact format. An annual gathering of bell ringers from the Granada coast, for example, would allow the few experts who still reside in the region to connect with others from the Alpujarra, the Axarquía, or the Campo de Gibraltar. The diversity of ringing styles between areas so geographically close yet so distinct in their history would add extra appeal, and the presence of outside visitors would help the residents of Almuñécar rediscover a heritage they have ignored for decades. The tower of the Church of la Encarnación, with its impressive set of bells, offers an ideal setting for such an initiative.

The case of Villavante also teaches that transmission cannot rely exclusively on individual goodwill. The Leonese bell ringers have understood that they need minimal support structures: a fixed calendar, a meeting place, communication channels, and, above all, recognition from local institutions. In Almuñécar, none of these pieces are in place. The local bell ringers have no space to meet, they are not included in the municipality's cultural program, and they have not received any proposals to document their ringing or teach it to younger generations.

The comparison between the two towns is not intended to idealize the Leonese model or present Almuñécar as a lost cause. Villavante has made mistakes, gone through years of low participation, and had to adapt to the demographic changes in the rural environment. However, its persistence demonstrates that collective organization can halt, and even reverse, the loss of a sonic language that seemed doomed to disappear. Almuñécar has historical bells, bell ringers who still remember the tolls for the dead, for festivals, and for alarms, and a social fabric dense enough to sustain an annual gathering if someone were to take the first step.

That first step, according to the experience of Villavante, is usually the hardest. It requires overcoming inertia, getting past the feeling that it is already too late, and convincing the bell ringers themselves that their knowledge deserves to be shared. In the Leonese town, the promoters of the gathering recall that at first many veterans were reluctant: they did not understand why anyone would want to learn ringing that they themselves had practiced out of obligation, without any glamour. The answer came when the first young people approached with genuine curiosity and the veterans discovered that their knowledge, far from being a relic of the past, aroused admiration and respect.

Almuñécar has the opportunity to replicate this dynamic, adapting it to its coastal reality and its festive calendar. A bell ringers' gathering held in spring or autumn, away from the tourist saturation of summer, could become a modest but significant event within the cultural landscape of the Costa Tropical. The raw materials exist: bells, bell ringers, history, and a potential audience that, as Villavante demonstrates, responds when offered the opportunity to listen and learn. What is missing is the decision to convene, to open the tower, and to trust that the sound of the bells still has something to say.
